title: Whaling
summary: Whaling history on Native Long Island connects whales as living relations, drift-whale harvests, seventeenth-century shore-whaling labor, Shinnecock, Montaukett, and Unkechaug maritime skill, industrial whaling, ecological loss, and present-day whale conservation.
activity_update_summary: Removed an accidentally appended draft maritime article and repeated source tail; retained the complete cited Whaling article and connected Historic Moments.
why_this_matters: Whaling history shows Native Long Island as a maritime homeland shaped by reciprocal relationships with whales, skilled Native labor, colonial exploitation, global travel, and present-day responsibility to living whale populations.
history_content:
Whales, Kinship, and the Shore

Whaling history on Long Island begins before the commercial industry. Indigenous communities along the Atlantic shore knew whales as powerful beings, food, material support, and relatives in a living coastal world. A stranded or drift whale could feed many people, provide oil and bone, and call for ceremony, distribution, and respect. Shinnecock oral history remembered this abundance in plain terms: the whale was to coastal Native people what the buffalo was to Plains peoples.12

The evidence is strongest for careful use of drift or beached whales and for nearshore practices, including work with smaller whales or calves in shallow bays. Claims that Long Island Native people regularly hunted large whales in the open ocean before European contact should be stated cautiously. Archaeologists and historians have debated that question because the Long Island record does not provide the same kind of precontact open-ocean whaling evidence found in some other regions.18

Nineteenth-century East Hampton historian David L. Gardiner described Montaukett thanksgiving feasts connected with whales, especially the fins and tails. That account is not the same as a Native-authored ceremony record, but it is important because seventeenth-century Long Island deeds also show Native leaders reserving rights to the fins and tails of stranded whales. Together, those records point to fins and tails as culturally important portions, not simply butchered meat.36

Seventeenth-Century Shore Whaling

English settlers quickly recognized that whale oil and baleen could become a profitable trade, but Native whalers held the local knowledge, winter surf skill, and boat-handling ability that made shore whaling possible. By the mid-seventeenth century, Southampton and East Hampton whaling companies supplied cedar boats, iron harpoons, tryworks, and trade goods while depending on Shinnecock, Montaukett, Unkechaug, and other Native men to do the most dangerous work at sea.14

Southampton records from 1643 show colonial anxiety over Robert Bond making harping irons for Native people. The town order treated whaling irons as weapons even while colonial businessmen needed Native crews to keep the fishery alive. That contradiction ran through the industry: colonists tried to restrict Native access to arms and metal while making exceptions when whaling profits required Native labor.14

Contracts from the 1670s show Shinnecock men such as Towsacum and Philip entering agreements with Southampton men, while Unkechaug whalers worked the Mastic and South Shore waters. Payment often came in coats, shoes, cloth, corn, tobacco, powder, shot, knives, rum, or a share of oil and bone. The system offered access to goods and wages, but it also tied many Native whalers to merchant credit, debt, and indenture. Native whalers still negotiated: they compared terms, sought better employers, and in 1676 Unkechaug men petitioned for their own whaling company so they would not have to work through English middlemen.145

Long Island Families and Whaling Records

Whaling records preserve Native names that otherwise might appear only briefly in colonial papers. Montaukett leader Wobetom appears in land, cattle, and whaling records; the Pantigo burial context linked his name to the material world of seventeenth-century East Hampton. Wyandanch's transfer of drift-whale rights to Lion Gardiner, while reserving the fins and tails, shows how whale rights were part of diplomacy, land pressure, and Native political authority.6

Unkechaug whaling history is especially visible in the Pigskin Book, the Smith family account ledger from 1696 to 1721. That ledger names more than thirty Native whalers and shows how deeply shore whaling was woven into labor, debt, household survival, and colonial power around the Mastic peninsula.5

For Shinnecock families, whaling remained a major part of public memory into the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The Lee family, including Shinnecock whalemen such as Milton, Ferdinand, Notley, James, and Garrison Lee, shows Native maritime skill in a later deep-sea industry that reached far beyond Long Island. Their work was not local isolation; it connected Shinnecock homes to Sag Harbor, New Bedford, the Arctic, the Pacific, and other global whaling grounds.72

From Shore Whaling to Industry

By the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, shore whaling had become a business across eastern Long Island. Southampton organized communal responsibility for trying whales cast up by the sea in the 1640s, and by the late 1600s East Hampton and Southampton companies were investing in whaling crews. As nearshore right whales declined and avoided the coast, voyages moved farther offshore, requiring larger vessels, ports, and capital.14

Sag Harbor grew into one of the major American whaling ports of the nineteenth century. The industry supported shipbuilding, coopering, sail-making, chandlery, waterfront labor, and merchant wealth. Native whalers entered that world as skilled seamen, boatsteerers, harpooners, and officers, not only as anonymous laborers. Montaukett and Shinnecock men traveled through the Atlantic, Arctic, South America, and the Pacific and returned with wages, objects, stories, and wider kinship connections.278

This was also an extractive industry that turned Native knowledge into capitalist profit and helped destroy whale populations. The same story can hold both truths: Native whalers exercised skill, agency, and mobility, while colonial and later industrial whaling depended on unequal contracts, debt, racial hierarchy, and the mass killing of whales.128

Decline, Loss, and Survivance

By the late nineteenth century, petroleum, changing markets, overhunting, and depleted whale populations pushed the Long Island whaling economy into decline. Native workers shifted toward fishing, guiding, the U.S. Life-Saving Service, domestic work, crafts, seasonal labor, and other forms of wage work. Whaling did not disappear from memory: it remained in family stories, public commemorations, art, place histories, and biographies of Shinnecock, Montaukett, and Unkechaug people.78

The 1876 Circassian shipwreck is part of that history. Ten Shinnecock men drowned after going to salvage the stranded ship off the East End. The tragedy belongs to maritime labor history as well as whaling memory, because it shows the ongoing risk that Native men faced in winter surf and coastal work after the height of the whale fishery.7

Whales Today

Today, the relationship is not a continuation of the commercial whaling industry. Contemporary Native reflections in Shoemaker's oral histories distinguish older Indigenous responsibilities to whales from the market industry that decimated whale populations. Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile and Holly Haile Davis described prayer, song, grief, and respect for stranded whales, while also speaking against the exploitation that reduced living whale nations to oil, bone, and profit.2

That distinction matters now because whales are still in Long Island and Northeast waters, and many still face human-caused threats. NOAA lists entanglement, vessel strikes, ocean noise, habitat degradation, shifting prey, and changing ocean conditions among the major dangers to North Atlantic right whales. NOAA's marine mammal stranding program treats strandings as events that can reveal disease, vessel strike, fishing gear entanglement, pollution, noise, and larger ocean-health problems.913

Current Whale Numbers

Population numbers depend on species, stock, survey area, and survey year. For the North Atlantic right whale, NOAA describes the species as one of the world's most endangered large whales and gives a current abundance of approximately 380 whales, with only about 70 reproductively active females. The 2023 NOAA stock assessment, using photographic information through November 30, 2023, estimated 372 adult and subadult western North Atlantic right whales and a minimum population estimate of 367.9

For humpback whales, NOAA treats populations by distinct population segments and stocks. The Gulf of Maine stock assessment's best abundance estimate was 1,396 whales, based on photo-identification histories through October 2016. NOAA also notes that commercial whaling severely reduced humpbacks, that the International Whaling Commission moratorium beginning in the mid-1980s was central to recovery, and that some populations have recovered while others remain endangered or threatened.10

For fin whales in the western North Atlantic, NOAA's 2023 stock assessment gives a best current abundance estimate of 6,802 and a minimum estimate of 5,573. Fin whales remain listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act and depleted under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. For sperm whales in the North Atlantic, NOAA's 2023 stock assessment states that there is no reliable estimate for the entire North Atlantic, but the best recent estimate for surveyed U.S. Western North Atlantic waters is 5,895, with a minimum estimate of 4,639. Sperm whales remain endangered and depleted while recovering from commercial whaling.1112

Why This History Matters

Whaling on Native Long Island is not one story. It is a story of kinship with whales, careful use of stranded whales, ceremony, Native maritime skill, colonial dependence on Indigenous labor, debt, global travel, family survival, ecological loss, and present-day responsibility. Seeing the whole arc keeps the history from turning Native whalers into either romantic figures or exploited labor alone. It also keeps whales in the story as living beings whose current survival remains tied to human choices.12913
